content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for ackowledging the analytical results. Please see below our response to the concerns:

   * $\textbf{Relation\ to\ previous\ works\ for\ NNs}$: As outlined in the Introduction, there exists no optimization results on DeepONets and therefore the present proofs present a first step in understanding the optimization landscape of DeepOnets. We believe the novelty is in the model itself. Our analysis for DeepONets is simpler than that of Du et al. 2019 for neural networks. 

   * $\textbf{Operator\ Learning}$: The Operator Learning problem is in sharp contrast to standard supervised learning for neural networks
and therefore we strongly believe that it warrants a separate analysis. 

In addition to the above, establishing the necessary conditions in Section 4 (RSC, RSS and restricted PL) is highly nontrivial for the DeepONet model.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5740 by Reviewer BsC5

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for bringing out several interesting observations. Please see our response to each of the concerns below: 

   * $\textbf{Relation\ to\ FNO}$: We would like to to reiterate the point presented in Introduction. “While constructing such neural operators constitutes a large body of work in itself, to the best of our knowledge, none of the preceding works have provided convergence guarantees on when and why these neural operators/operator networks and their underlying optimization algorithms converge to the global optimum"

The above is true for both FNO and DeepONet which are two popular classes of Neural Operators / Operator networks that each warrant a separate analysis due to their distinct features. We do not make any claims comparing FNO with DeepONet, nor do we feel such claims to be relevant to the analysis we have presented. 

To summarize, in this work we have established provable guarantees for the convergence of GD for DeepONet, which is a first work of its kind. A similar analysis for FNO, while possible, is outside the scope of this work.


   * $\textbf{Overparameterization\ helps\ DeepONets}$: We again thank the reviewer for bringing an important point to our attention. While there exists a wealth of literature on overparameterization for Neural Networks (that approximate “functions”), there exists no work that provably demonstrates the effect of overparameterization for Neural Operators / Operator Networks.


   * $\textbf{Operator\ Perspective\ and\ Proof\ technique}$: The operator perspective is a result of the approximation guarantees of DeepONets. It is baked into the Universal Approximation Theorem for Operators in the original DeepONet paper (Lu et al., 2021). In this work we analyze the corresponding neural model for DeepONet and establish convergence guarantees for that model. The proof technique showing the RSC of the DeepONet loss and the positive-definiteness of the DeepONet-NTK are both novel and establish a first result that shows convergence of gradient descent for the corresponding operator learning problem. 


   * $\textbf{Analogy\ to\ ResNets}$: A ResNet is a fundamentally different model than DeepONet. The former approximates mapping between two finite-dimensional vector spaces. This is in sharp contrast to DeepONet which takes in as input both the input (which is a function discretized on a grid) and also the output locations (where the corresponding solution needs to be queried) and as a result learns mappings between two function spaces. 

This is fundamentally different from a standard ResNet. In fact, a ResNet maybe used as a sub-architecture (for the branch and/or trunk net) instead of a FNN. However, that analysis is again outside the scope of this work. 

   * $\textbf{Experimental Observations}$: We feel that the experiments communicate the main story fairly succinctly and complement the
theoretical results, which, as the reviewer correctly points out, are the heart of the paper. Hence, we believe that they should be placed in the main paper to elucidate the main technical results succinctly.


   * $\textbf{Novelty}$: We would like to further reiterate that DeepONets do not have any optimization guarantees and establishing these is the main technical result of our paper. The analysis presented in the paper builds on top of existing results for neural networks and extends these to Operator Networks.

Technically, the authors prove the convergence for both smooth activations and ReLU activation and show that a linear convergence rate can be achieved. The authors further present empirical results to back up the theoretical findings.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. This paper proves the convergence for DeepONets with smooth activations based on the RSC condition.
2. This paper proves the convergence for DeepONets with ReLU activation based on the NTK analysis.
3. This paper conducts numerical experiments to justify the theory.

weakness:
1. The initialization of weights in Assumption 3 seems unreasonable to me. In fact, the authors consider using a small scaling for only the last layer, then the optimization on the last layer weights will dominate the training of the remaining weights. By (5), the neural network model will be very close to the linear model. 
2. It is also not clear to me why the authors need to use two sections to study the convergence of DeepONets with two different types of activations. My understanding is that they can be both performed via standard NTK analysis (in the lazy training regime, there is nearly no difference between NTK and RSC based analysis).
3. In the ReLU case, it would be better to give a quantitative bound on $\lambda_{0,g}$  or $c$ in Theorem 5.1.

content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I am not satisfied with the initialization in Assumption 3, the authors may need to make the training of all layers be in the same level rather than using different initialization scaling for different layers. Besides, the contributions of this paper are not strong, especially given a large number of prior works studying the convergence of GD in the NTK regime.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for raising this point and in the process helping us spot a typo in equations (4) and (5). We would like to bring clarity regarding Assumption 3: 

   * $\textbf{Assumption\ 3}$: Note that the scaling of the last layer is identical to the previous layers except for an additional factor of $1/K$. The $1/K$ is to take into account the $K$-predictors in the branch net in $\sum\limits_{k=1}^K f_k g_k$. Note that in the previous layers the $1/\sqrt{m}$ is explicitly multiplied with the weight matrices $W^{(l)}$, whereas for the last layer this is taken implicitly into account in the initialization variance (the $1/\sqrt{m}$ is pushed in the Gaussian to give a $1/m$ variance). We have also corrected equations (4) and (5) in light of the comment.



   * $\textbf{Two\ Different\ Sections}$: As for the necessity of two different analyses we remark that both the analyses establish sufficient conditions for the convergence of GD. The positive definiteness of the NTK and the RSC of the loss are distinct and independent from each other. Since either is a sufficient condition for convergence, we believe that these warrant separate sections in the main paper.

   * $\textbf{Quantitative\ Bound\ for\ }\ \lambda_{\min}$:  A bound on the minimum eigenvalues of the branch $\lambda_{0,f}$ and trunk $\lambda_{0, g}$ nets could be given in the same spirit as [Nguyen et al. 2021]. In particular, 

        * $\lambda_{0,f}= \min\limits_{k\in [K]} {\lambda^{(k)}_{0,f}}$ 
        * $\lambda_{0,g}= \min\limits_{k\in [K]}{\{\lambda^{(k)}_{0,g}\}}$

where each of the above minima are the minimum eigenvalues of the limiting tangent kernels associated with the $K$ branch and trunk net predictors respectively. These can be suitably bounded from below. While the bounds aren't sharp, these suffice for the current analysis. Since the proof follows directly from Nguyen et al. 2021, we have not reproduced it as is, and have added reference to Theorem 4.1 in Nguyen et al., 2021 in the updated draft.

content.title: Convergence results
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for raising several important points. Our response along with corresponding updates to the draft above is detailed below.

   * While the approach using NTK in Section 5 would apply to both smooth and ReLU activations, the Hessian-based approach does not directly apply to ReLU. The Hessian-based analysis, however, provides a sufficient condition for the convergence of gradient descent for the DeepONet learning problem. We have now included this as a footnote in the main paper on page 7. 

   * The width $m$ controls the extent of restricted strong convexity (RSC) of the loss (Theorem 4.2). We $\bf do\ not\ show\ nor\ use$ any form of strong convexity (whether local or global) for the DeepONet loss. From the outset, we consider only $\alpha$-RSC and provably demonstrate the RSC of the loss with the parameter $\alpha \equiv \alpha(m)$.

To summarize, we do not guarantee local convexity for the DeepONet loss and only show α-RSC.

   * Positive definiteness of the NTK at initialization:  We build the intuition in light of Assumption 3. Since the branch and trunk nets are simple feedforward networks with the parameters initialized according to Assumption 3, the NTK corresponding to each of them is positive definite. This follows directly from previous works [Du et al., 2019; Nguyen et al., 2019;]. Furthermore, since the DeepONet model is an inner product of K-predictors (the K branch and trunk net outputs) the combined NTK would "likely" be positive definite. The intuition, however, isn't sufficient and indeed we show explicitly via Theorem 5.1 (proof in in Appendix A.4) and propositions 2, 3, 4, that the resulting DeepONet NTK is positive-definite.

The result holds irrespective of $u$ being an identity function or not.


   * Indeed the loss is $\alpha$-RSC w.r.t. (Q, θ). The note above (14) is merely an elaboration of the definition of Restricted Strong Convexity (RSC) and its distinction from Strong Convexity (SC). We appreciate the reviewer for spotting out the typo in the definition of $\bar{G}_t$ and have now corrected it.

replying_to: Replying to Learning Deep Operator Networks: The Benefits of Over-Parameterization

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
The paper establishes convergence guarantees on using gradient descent. for training Deep Operator Networks (DeepONets) in the over-parameterized regime. Two settings are studied: smooth activations (for which the convergence proofs are based on a restricted strong convexity/PL-type analysis), and ReLU activations (for which the proofs are based on NTK). 

Opinions were split about this paper. In terms of strengths, most reviewers (including this meta-reviewer) thought that the paper was generally well-written and that the results were sound. The fact that DeepONets are becoming popular in the numerical analysis/PDE literature is also indicative of possible impact.

However, several weaknesses were also highlighted. The literature on provable training of over-parameterized networks is quite mature by now. A majority of reviewers pointed out the new proofs were more of an application of a well-worn set of analysis techniques (RSC, NTK) for a slightly more complex neural network architecture, rather than providing any special new insights. This meta-reviewer concurs with this view. Moreover, one reviewer pointed out that the effect of over-parameterization was not particularly well-illuminated. The authors' response pointed out the dependence between the RSC constant and the width, but this meta-reviewer believes that more can/should be said here about the "benefits of over-parameterization", as the paper title suggests. Finally, some concerns were raised about the assumption of non-uniform scaling of different layers at initialization, which is non-standard in practice.

Overall, this is a good paper but possibly falls short of the (very) high bar for acceptance set at this year's ICLR. 

Recommendation: (weak) reject.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: As expressed in the summary above, the paper has several positive aspects, but on the balance this meta-reviewer feels that they are outweighed by the negatives.
content.justification_for_why_not_lower_score: Despite the fact that the paper follows a well-trodden path in analyzing over-parameterized networks, the contributions are clearly expressed and (to the best of our knowledge) new to the literature.
